Dijkstra's Dining Philosophers problem, in which five philosophers alternately think and eat using forks shared with their neighbors, is the classic illustration of which concurrency problem?
choices: A buffer overflow from writing past the end of an allocated array
A stack overflow from excessive recursive calls
A race condition, where the result depends on unpredictable timing of reads and writes
Deadlock: each philosopher waits forever for a fork held by a neighbor who is also waiting, so no one can proceed

A machine learning model achieves 100% accuracy on the data it was trained on, but only 52% accuracy (barely better than a coin flip) on new, unseen data. What does this gap most likely indicate?
choices: 52% accuracy on unseen data is impossible if training accuracy is 100%, so there must be a bug in how accuracy is measured

The model has overfit the training data — it memorized specifics of the training set (including its noise) rather than learning patterns that generalize, so a perfect training score alone is not evidence of a good model
The training data must have been mislabeled
The model is actually performing excellently, since 100% is the best possible score on any dataset

questions.q: If a single farmer doubles their wheat output while every other farmer's output stays the same, that farmer's income rises. Does it follow that if ALL farmers simultaneously double their output, total income across the whole industry also rises?
choices: No, because wheat prices never change regardless of how much is supplied
Yes — more total wheat sold at the same price means more total income
No — when all farmers increase output together, the extra supply drives the market price down, and total industry income can actually fall, even though it rises for any single farmer acting alone
Yes, but only if demand for wheat triples as well

questions.q: A researcher runs 20 completely independent statistical tests on data where NO real effects exist (every null hypothesis is true), using the standard significance threshold of p < 0.05 for each individual test. Approximately what is the probability that AT LEAST one test comes back 'statistically significant' purely by chance?
choices: About 100%, since running enough tests guarantees a significant result
About 5%, since the significance threshold is fixed at 5% no matter how many tests you run
About 25%, roughly five times the base 5% risk
About 64%, because the chance of avoiding a false positive shrinks with every additional independent test run

questions.q: A turkey is fed by the farmer every single day for 1,000 days, and each day its confidence that 'the farmer will feed me again tomorrow, since he always has' grows statistically stronger based on the data. On day 1,001 — the day before Thanksgiving — its confidence is at its highest point ever. That is the day the farmer kills it. What does this illustrate?
choices: That turkeys simply aren't intelligent enough to make valid statistical inferences, unlike humans in similar situations

Past stability and a long track record can mask a qualitatively different, catastrophic event that hasn't happened yet — and more confirming data can make that event feel even less likely right up until it happens; this is Nassim Taleb's 'turkey problem', an example of a black swan event
That you should always trust a long, unbroken track record as a reliable predictor of the future
The farmer's behavior was random, so no inference was ever justified in the first place

questions.q: A map shows that 6 cancer cases happen to cluster within 2 blocks of a particular cell tower, in a large city where cases are otherwise scattered essentially at random. A campaign cites this cluster as proof the tower causes cancer. What is the key flaw in treating this single cluster as evidence of causation?
choices: None — if a cluster exists, there must be a shared physical cause
6 cases is simply too small a number to ever be meaningful, regardless of location

The 'Texas sharpshooter fallacy': drawing the target (the region of interest) after seeing where the cases already landed — cherry-picking an apparent cluster that random chance alone would be expected to produce somewhere in a large enough area
The cluster is irrelevant, because cancer is never caused by environmental factors

questions.q: Which is the better deal: one 12-inch pizza for $10, or two 6-inch pizzas for the same $10 total (all diameters, same thickness and toppings)?
choices: The two 6-inch pizzas — more pieces means more food
The 12-inch pizza — it has double the area of the two 6-inch pizzas combined
The two 6-inch pizzas — smaller pizzas have less wasted crust
They are exactly the same amount of pizza
